item.title: Why I Stopped Using AI Code Editors — 2026 (A Look Back from April 2025)
item.description:
In early April 2025, I posted a translation on Habr of Luciano Nooijen's note "Why I Stopped Using AI Code Editors" (original from April 1, 2025). I was publishing the translation between code reviews: while agents wrote code for a couple of projects, I checked diffs every few minutes and gave clarifying tasks. In the same post, I wrote about our long walks in Samui with a friend, a very cool coder I look up to — 0xhyperdust. We discussed a lot about what our favorite activity would become in a few years and what to do right now to remain in demand. The main hypothesis was that in 2-3 years, we would become AI operators, tasked with understanding the global and local logic of projects, setting tasks, writing architectural code sections, and intervening when something goes wrong. Luciano's article proposed the opposite view: remove LLM integrations from the editor and only interact with models manually to avoid losing skills. In the end, the post gathered 26 comments and 303 votes in a poll about how many programmers would remain in a couple of years. Now, in October 2026, I've reread both the translation and the entire thread under it. The irony is that today I literally agree with Luciano's title: I no longer need AI code editors. Only the reason is different. Instead of a code editor with autocompletion and a side chat, there are now agent wrappers where we work as orchestrators. More precisely, the human in this scheme is one of the orchestrators. Read more

item.title: How AI Agents are Helping in Manufacturing
item.description:
I've already pondered whether AI could replace engineers. Now, I propose looking at the work it's already taking on and the practical results. I'm particularly interested in cases where the AI agent's work can be verified on a real part: measuring warpage after casting, testing strength, comparing temperature under load. Or simply calculating the time spent on production preparation and how many engineering hours were saved. Let's examine ten examples from publications in August-October 2026. These include metal processing, plastic molding, 3D printing, battery testing, and electronics cooling. The readiness level varies: some parts have already been manufactured, some have had samples printed and tested, and some have only shown simulation experiments. However, these examples clearly show the engineering work agents are beginning to take on. Images generated by AI based on each topic to slightly diversify the article's text. 1. item.title: SIEM on Two Cores for 150 Hosts and a 9B Model for Triage: How a Custom AI SOC Works
item.description:
Imagine a SOC where a language model analyzes every triggered rule. Ideally, it correctly handles about 60% of second-line events. The remaining 40% are false positives and misses, making automatic response impossible. Alexander Kelchin's team, CTO and CISO of Medici Lab, arrived at this figure through their own experiments. They then rebuilt their SIEM so that a 9-billion-parameter model achieved 96-97% correct answers, while the entire system handled 150 hosts on two CPU cores. Read more

item.title: How I made a cartoon about the kitten FyrFyr - 80 seconds in 30 minutes on Sol 6.1
item.description:
I looked at my notes and realized they were a mess of terms. How would I explain this to my grandmother? For example, vector cartoons on JavaScript/HTML, which neural networks now create at a speed of 1:30 (one minute of animation in half an hour) and at a negligible cost. How would I explain why I'm so happy? Hello, Grandma, I've learned to make cartoons with a neural network. No, not like movies with Stirlitz and kittens that talk and walk on their hind legs. These are special neural networks, they draw cool, but they are expensive, you see? You could go broke if you wanted to draw yourself. But here I open it and type on my computer - make me a cartoon like for children. Not realistic, yes, drawn. But it's very cheap - yesterday I made minute-long videos on Claude Opus 5.5, and then on ChatGPT Sol 6.1 - it cost pennies, half an hour of work. The weekly limit was practically not used, Opus used a maximum of 10 percent. Here's an example - Kitten FyrFyr - not to be confused with the kitten named Gav. Watch the kitten animated in JS

item.title: AI Assistant for 1C Learns to Analyze Code and Update Customizations in Extensions
item.description:
The main scenario used to be: a user connects AI to an information base, asks a question, and gets an answer based on its data. Recent versions have added capabilities for maintenance and development tasks: finding the cause of a document's behavior, checking method intercepts, or preparing an extension modification. The "ChatGPT, Codex + Claude for 1C" solution now includes tools for analyzing program code, creating and modifying extensions, and verifying customizations after updating the standard configuration. Direct connection from ChatGPT and anonymization of supported personal data before sending to the model have also been added. Configuration and extension code analysis: The assistant can now find procedures and functions, navigate call chains, and correlate program logic with actual information base data. For example, a developer can ask: "Why does the project change when this document is posted?" For such analysis, the program creates a local index of modules in the main configuration and active extensions. This allows finding relevant code snippets without constantly exporting the entire configuration to files. The AI receives the code fragments necessary for the task. Indexing is done in read-only mode and does not alter the working configuration. Creating and modifying extensions: Using Codex and Claude, you can create extensions and modify the code of existing ones. The program applies prepared changes in the database and restarts 1C. Extension versions are saved, allowing you to revert to a previous state. Read more

item.title: InkPeek — a translator for Android e-readers: works offline, and with internet, it explains via AI
item.description:
Hello. This is a post about a small application I made for myself. I'll say right away: I wrote it with a neural network. I don't know how Habr feels about such projects now, but maybe someone will find it useful. I wanted to read more books in a foreign language - on an e-reader, of course. But I couldn't find a convenient dictionary for my e-reader that would instantly translate a word or phrase over the page, and with an internet connection, also explain the grammar. AI plugins for KOReader are overloaded, and dictionaries for FBReader look like a relic from the early 2000s. So I made my own. It works on e-readers like Boox: it connects to FBReader, CoolReader, or KOReader as an external dictionary and is called from the text selection menu, online and offline. Initially, it was an experiment, but it stuck with me, so I decided to share it. How it works

item.title: AI Agent Security: More Oversight or a Dedicated Environment?
item.description:
TL;DR. On October 19th, Microsoft stated that internal agents should be treated as insiders without a presumption of trust. Their proposal: "supervisor" agents that monitor every action of every agent before it happens. I agree with the diagnosis but doubt the prescription. The post mentions "overprivileged," and I believe that's the core issue: agents are given excessive permissions because precise delegation is impossible—permissions are scattered across systems with no unified model. My hypothesis: some oversight can be replaced by structuring the agent's operating environment. A supervisor treats the symptom by observing an action and guessing its intent. If permissions, data, and relationships are described in a single model, an agent can be granted specific user permissions, leaving little to guess, thus requiring less oversight. Below, I explore how known agent incidents would play out in such an environment and what deterministic tests of our core have revealed. Read on.

item.title: AI Can Jump
item.description:
This year, it seems we've definitively moved into AI-assisted coding, and there's no turning back. For me personally, it's hard to imagine giving up AI – I'm hooked. But until recently, I couldn't quite grasp why some developers claim AI writes all their code, leaving them with nothing to do, while others insist AI is merely an assistant whose code needs careful review. And then there are those who are completely disillusioned with AI, using it more as a reference than a full-fledged development tool. Read on
